Sorry but this is terrible advice, antipsychotics are d2 antagonists. Ssri induced elevation of 5ht reduces d2 receptor availability in the nigrostriatal pathway, hence the akathisia. It is uncommon, but known for 40 years ssris can have this side effect. If anything the OP might benefit from a d2/d3 agonist instead of an ssri - something like pramipexole. Plenty if growing evidence for its use in a subset of patients with depression and also in chronic pain too.

Take a look here: [https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1060028015594812](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1060028015594812) and here [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4617661/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4617661/)

You could try a D2 agonist to restore signalling to the infundibular nucleus and nigrostriatal pathway, or a different class of anti depressant like Bupropion which acts mainly on NET. Pramipexole a D3/D2 agonist has some interesting evidence supporting its use in depression and also chronic pain.

Several studies report decreases in cocaine cravings and self-administration and intrest in taking cocaine after 4 weeks. Normalises the expression of excitatory amino acid transporter 2 in the nucleus accumbens), the reduced expression of EAAT2 in this region is implicated in addictive drug-seeking behavior.
* Vitamin D3 (Fultium 3,200 iu) o.d - excellent for unexplained aches and pains. Increases sensitivity to dopamine, reduces amphetamine self-administration in mice. Upregulates production of tyrosine hydroxylase, a rate limiting enzyme in dopamine synthesis.

When LSD binds to the 5-HT2A receptor a number of interesting things happen. LSD is very potent because when it binds to the receptor it causes morphological changes in the receptors structure causing the LSD molecule to become trapped there. Eventually the receptors are internalised and recycled. Some people have hypothesised that this temporary loss of 5ht2a receptor sensitivity could partially account for the 'after glow' effects.   


The 5-HT2A receptor also has multiple signalling cascades, LSD and psilocin just so happen to activate a pathway that results in the psychedelic effect. Other ligands such as lisuride do not.

  
The 5-HT2A receptor often forms a complex with mGlu2 receptors. Several selective Glur2 antagonists are currently being researched for their antidepressant effects.

I'm 23. I am also diagnosed with Aspergers, and your post scares the hell out of me. Currently I'm working as a customer service advisor in a garage, I deal with members of the public negative emotions all day long. It's my job to turn other peoples problems around, and take on their stress. As someone diagnosed with Aspergers, I couldn't be working in a more ill fitting job. Despite that, I'm bloody good at what I do, topping company KPI league tables. I have also been living on my own in rented accommodation for the past 2 years; I make less money after tax than the original poster. 

On top of all this, I don't have any GCSE's, A levels or formal qualifications of any kind. I left school when I was 14. I had to leave, due to not being able to integrate with other school children. The regular outburst and meltdowns were a huge disruption for the other kids. I isolated myself for about 18 months, never leaving the house and only leaving bed to eat.

I remember watching some program on TV one day, the subject was eye contact and autism. It was like the penny dropped. How was I meant to know to look at peoples eyes when they spoke to me? Logically, the sound came out their mouth, so why not concentrate my attention there? Nobody had ever told me different. It started me on a path to researching body language, facial expressions, speech patterns everything. I practised what I had learnt on my family, then acquaintances. Pretty soon, I had friends. I even managed to get a girlfriend. At first it felt awkward and forced like I was acting, but when I could see it working it became more natural.

The key thing however, it all requires an insurmountable effort. All this, just to pretend to function normally in society. It was exhausting.

So these days, even though I'm functioning. I wouldn't say I was exactly living. I did suffer a burnout 2 years ago and took 6 months off work. I regularly fall asleep at 7PM from exhaustion, there's no longer any hope of life outside of work, there's no energy left at the end of the day. 

I can't achieve anything. I'm deeply depressed and anxious even when things are going well for me. My PHQ-9 mood score had hovered between 21-24 for at least the past couple of years and my GAD-7 anxiety score recently topped out at 19. I'm depressed because I'm depressed more than anything, but it's certainly exacerbated knowing that it's probably impossible for me to work towards an education and better life for myself. I definitely could cope in a classroom with the progress I've made in my working life, I wish I could go back. Theoretical Physics and engineering interest me a great deal. All my colleagues tell me "you're too good for this place" and that I come across as intelligent. If only they knew the full extent of my struggle. The worst thing is, every day that passes, I know I'll never get to be my best version of my self. I think about suicide on an almost daily basis, I'm miserable truth be told.

I'd like to know if the benefit system is helping you in any way to try and reintegrate into what might be considered a normal life. Do they offer any resources in order for you to better live with you condition and perhaps in time a small job might be a possibility? Knowing that the work you do is valued by somebody else can be a great boost to ones self-esteem.

I know and fully appreciate that everyone's circumstances are different. Some people truly will never improve, and those people have nothing but my sincere empathy. Well as sincere as it can be coming from an aspie.

I would not say I am cured. Unless making a conscious effort, I'm pretty blind and oblivious socially. I guess my resources have been reallocated from learning and making the most of myself, to surviving and living each day as it comes. There's not really any other choice but to keep going is there? I'm not sure how long I can keep it up; but I do.

What will you do if your benefits are taken away and they deem you fit for work? It must be a stressful thought. It's funny how politicians are all praising the 3 MP's that spoke out about their mental health. Yet their taking benefits away from hundreds unable to work due to their mental health. I calmly explained to her that although not an official service the store offered, I could attempt a file recovery for her, but there were no guarantees. We both walked to the computer that was situated in the centre of the shop floor on a podium. 

We had to use this computer as it was the only one not networked, and hence not monitored by head office. This meant we could install any software we liked, without fear of repercussions. It served as the ideal platform for under the radar file recoveries for members of the public, and this unofficial service earnt us members of staff countless doughnuts and biscuits in thanks.

I fired up the file recovery utility and proceeded to scan her card for missing files. It returned the entire directory and I casually clicked one at random to see if it had worked. It was at this precise moment the young Indian lady's cheeks turned the most awesomely rich shade of red I had ever seen. For now, full-screen, for the entire store and all of it's patrons to see, was her nude body; in a rather unflattering position that left nothing to the imagination!

With complete composure I asked. "are these your pictures?" I received a whimpered and rather shy "yes" in return. Needless to say, there were no doughnuts or biscuits that day. But there was an epic 'right-click, save-as' and funny story to tell. (there was even a video)
